topic: Searching an archive that misreads its own words
grammarFocus: 学术论证的限定、因果、对比与证据范围
title: Searching an archive that misreads its own words
instructions: 原创学术微训练；场景、机构与数值均为虚构模拟，不是事实报道或官方试题。先独立阅读答题，再用原句核对限定、比较与因果。短篇专项不能替代完整陌生测评。
passage:
A. A fictional town archive scanned a set of handwritten shop ledgers. The resulting images were clear enough to read, but searching them required text produced by optical character recognition. The archive advertised a search for every mention of bicycle repairs. A local historian welcomed easier access while warning that a search could return only the words the software had recognised.

B. In several ledgers, faded ink made the word bicycle resemble another sequence of letters. Those entries remained visible in the page images but were absent from a keyword search. A low result count therefore did not establish that few repairs had occurred. Nor did every returned result represent a relevant event: some entries described the sale of a bicycle rather than its repair.

C. The historian checked a sample of pages selected by page number, rather than by search result. This allowed her to find relevant entries the search had missed. She classified errors as omissions or false matches. The two categories mattered because improving one could worsen the other. A looser search might recover damaged spellings but also return more irrelevant words.

D. The archive considered asking volunteers to correct the transcription. It proposed preserving the original machine output beside the corrected version. Each correction would be linked to a page image and a dated record of the change. Users could then distinguish a reading supported by clear handwriting from one that remained doubtful. The aim was not to make every uncertainty disappear behind a clean-looking search screen.

E. For the exhibition, the archive showed an image, the machine reading and a corrected line together. It also explained that the ledgers covered only participating shops. Even a perfect transcription would not record repairs done at home or at businesses whose books had not survived. Better retrieval could improve access to the archive without turning that archive into a complete history of the town. The historian's report kept technological accuracy separate from the completeness of the surviving evidence.
